Hospital day 4 rheumatology follow-up for a 78-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 25 years ago, admitted with a lupus flare. On admission she had several days of painful swollen joints in both hands and wrists, a facial rash, and fatigue. Overnight she had no fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath. This morning she says her joint pain is better and her morning stiffness is shorter, about 20 minutes. She denies oral ulcers, visual changes, blood in the urine, and abdominal pain.

Current medications are hydroxychloroquine 200 mg once daily, which she has taken for years, amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension, and pantoprazole 40 mg daily started on admission for stomach protection while on high-dose steroids. Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily was given for the first three days. Mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily was started yesterday.

Vitals today: Temp 36.9 C, BP 138/76, HR 76, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air. She is comfortable. There is a faint malar erythema that is fading. No oral ulcers. There is mild synovitis with swelling and tenderness in the MCP joints of both hands and the left wrist, involving fewer joints than on admission. Lungs are clear, the heart is regular with no rub, and there is no edema.

Lab review: WBC 3.9, hemoglobin 10.9, platelets 188, and creatinine 1.1 (baseline 1.0). Urinalysis shows 2+ protein with no red cell casts, and the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.9 g/g. C3 and C4 are low, anti-dsDNA is elevated at 1:640, and blood cultures remain negative.

My assessment is a systemic lupus erythematosus flare with polyarthritis and mucocutaneous involvement, improving on steroids, plus new proteinuria that is concerning for lupus nephritis. Her creatinine is near baseline.

For management, I am changing methylprednisolone to prednisone 40 mg by mouth daily today, with a planned taper of 5 mg per week once her symptoms and labs allow. Continue hydroxychloroquine 200 mg once daily, which is appropriate for her weight and kidney function, and she should have an annual retinal exam. Continue mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily and monitor her blood counts. Continue pantoprazole 40 mg daily while on steroids and continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. Nephrology consult to consider a renal biopsy. Repeat creatinine and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio in two days. Physical therapy for hand and wrist range of motion. Anticipate discharge in two to three days with rheumatology clinic follow-up in one week.

Hospitalist progress note dictation, hospital day 3, correction, hospital day 2. This is a 49-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration after three days of vomiting and watery diarrhea, presumed viral gastroenteritis. Her only chronic condition is hypertension. No acute events overnight. She says the vomiting has stopped and she had one loose stool yesterday, and she is tolerating a regular diet. She denies abdominal pain, fever, blood in the stool, and flank pain. She is very anxious this morning and asked many questions about whether her kidneys are permanently damaged, whether she will need dialysis, and when she can go home. I spent extra time answering each one and reassured her that this kind of injury usually recovers with fluids.

Current medications are normal saline at 125 mL per hour, and her home lisinopril 20 mg daily remains on hold since admission.

Vitals this morning, temperature 98.1, heart rate 82, down from 108 on admission, blood pressure 124/74, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Urine output was 1.4 liters over the last 24 hours. On exam her mucous membranes are moist, lungs are clear, abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no edema.

Labs this morning, creatinine 1.2, down from 2.1 on admission, with a baseline of 0.8. BUN 24, potassium 3.9, bicarbonate 22. Admission urinalysis showed concentrated urine without blood or protein.

My impression is prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration, improving, and hypertension. Going forward, continue normal saline until this evening, then stop and encourage oral fluids. Continue holding lisinopril until the creatinine returns to baseline. Repeat basic metabolic panel in the morning, avoid NSAIDs, and if the creatinine keeps improving she can go home tomorrow with repeat labs in one week.

Visit modality: telephone visit, audio only, with the patient at home. His identity was confirmed and he agreed to be seen by phone.

The patient is an 86-year-old male with benign prostatic hyperplasia who reports worsening urinary symptoms over the past 3 months. He describes a weak urinary stream, hesitancy, urinary frequency during the day, and nocturia with 3 trips to the bathroom each night. He denies burning with urination, blood in the urine, fever, and back pain. He has not had any episodes of urinary retention. His self-completed symptom score is 17, which is moderate, with a bother score of 4. He takes tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. He has a documented allergy to penicillin, which causes hives.

Home measurements: blood pressure 134/80 on his home cuff and pulse 72. No video was available, so no physical examination was performed; he sounds comfortable and speaks in full sentences on the phone.

Impression is benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms, only partly controlled on tamsulosin. Plan is to continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily and add finasteride 5 mg daily. A baseline PSA and urinalysis will be drawn at the lab before the first dose of finasteride. He should limit caffeine and evening fluids and avoid over-the-counter decongestants. Because of his penicillin allergy, a non-penicillin antibiotic will be chosen if a urinary tract infection is ever diagnosed. He will come in for a visit with a bladder scan for post-void residual in 3 months. He should call sooner or go to the emergency department if he cannot urinate, develops fever, or sees blood in his urine.

Doctor: Hi, I'm the emergency physician. I have you down as a 34-year-old female with severe right-sided pain, is that right?
Patient: Yes. It started this morning in my back on the right side and it comes in waves. It goes down toward my groin, and I threw up twice.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever and no chills.
Doctor: Any burning when you pee, or blood in the urine?
Patient: No burning, but my urine looked pink this morning.
Doctor: Have you ever had a kidney stone before?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Any medical problems, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: I have high blood pressure and I take lisinopril 10 mg every day.
Doctor: Any allergies to medications?
Patient: Yes, I'm allergic to ibuprofen. I get hives and my lips swell up.
Doctor: Thank you, that's important. I will not give you ibuprofen, ketorolac, or any other anti-inflammatory pain medicine. Is there any chance you could be pregnant?
Patient: No, my period ended last week.
Doctor: Okay, we will still do a urine pregnancy test. Your vitals when you came in were blood pressure 148/90, heart rate 98, temperature 98.2, and oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air. You look uncomfortable. On exam your abdomen is soft with mild tenderness on the right, and you have right flank tenderness. There is no rebound and no guarding.
Patient: It hurts when you press on my back there.
Doctor: Your urinalysis shows blood but no signs of infection, and your pregnancy test is negative. The CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis shows a 5 mm stone in the right ureter with mild swelling of the kidney, which is called hydronephrosis. Your creatinine is 0.9, so your kidney function is normal.
Patient: Okay. Can I get something for the pain? I feel sick to my stomach too.
Doctor: Yes. I am going to give you acetaminophen 1000 mg by IV, ondansetron 4 mg IV for the nausea, and morphine 4 mg IV for the severe pain.
Patient: Thank you.
Doctor: My impression is a kidney stone causing renal colic. A 5 mm stone has a good chance of passing on its own. You will go home with tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day to help the stone pass and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for pain. Drink plenty of fluids and strain your urine. Please follow up with urology in one week. Come back right away for fever, pain you cannot control, or if you cannot keep fluids down.
Patient: Okay, I understand.

Nephrology consultation. Requesting service is hospital medicine. Reason for consult is volume overload in a patient on maintenance hemodialysis.

HPI: This is a 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease from diabetic nephropathy on in-center hemodialysis three times weekly through a left arm arteriovenous fistula. He was admitted last night with shortness of breath and leg swelling. He returned about ten days ago from a three-week trip abroad, during which he completed only two dialysis sessions, and he admits to eating salty restaurant meals and drinking more fluids than usual. He estimates he has gained about 6 kg above his dry weight. He reports orthopnea and ankle swelling. He denies chest pain, fever, diarrhea, and cough. He still makes a small amount of urine.

Past history: end-stage renal disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Home medications are amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and sevelamer carbonate 800 mg three times daily with meals. No known drug allergies.

Exam: blood pressure 168/94, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 91% on 2 L nasal cannula, temperature 98.6 F. Elevated JVP, bibasilar crackles, and 2+ pitting edema to the knees. The fistula has a palpable thrill and audible bruit. There is no pericardial rub.

Data: potassium 5.8, sodium 134, hemoglobin 9.6. Chest x-ray shows pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG shows sinus rhythm without peaked T waves. Hepatitis B surface antigen was negative at the dialysis unit last month.

Impression: Volume overload from missed dialysis sessions and dietary sodium and fluid excess in end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. Mild hyperkalemia. Hypertension, likely volume-mediated.

Recommendations: Urgent hemodialysis tonight with an ultrafiltration goal of 3 to 4 liters as tolerated and a 2 potassium bath. Daily dialysis until he reaches his dry weight. Hold lisinopril while potassium is elevated. Continue amlodipine 10 mg daily and sevelamer carbonate 800 mg three times daily with meals. Strict intake and output, a low-salt diet, and a fluid restriction of 1 liter per day. Repeat BMP after dialysis. Supplemental oxygen to keep saturation above 92%. Given the recent international travel, recheck hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody per dialysis unit protocol and notify his outpatient unit before he returns. Social work to help arrange dialysis for future travel. We will follow daily.
